extracted.intended_audience: political campaign managers, public relations professionals, propagandists, statesmen
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning and executing political propaganda and public-relations campaigns: setting objectives, researching publics, budgeting, using emotions and media, training personnel, and institutionalizing public-relations functions in government and civic organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan campaign like big business
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire campaign should be worked out according to broad basic plans. Platforms, planks, pledges, budgets, activities, personalities, must be as carefully studied, apportioned and used as they are when big business desires to get what it wants from the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elaborate business methods and broad plans in political campaigning; prepare policies carefully and treat idea-selling as a large-scale business operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine objectives and express an honest platform
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step in a political campaign is to determine on the objectives, and to express them exceedingly well in the current form—that is, as a platform. In devising the platform the leader should be sure that it is an honest platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaign pledges and promises ought to carry something of the guarantee principle and money-back policy of an honorable business institution; avoid frivolous or insincere promises because the public has lost faith in campaign promotion work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a scientific analysis of the public
rubrics_metrics.description: To aid in the preparation of the platform there should be made as nearly scientific an analysis as possible of the public and of the needs of the public. A survey of public desires and demands would come to the aid of the political strategist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct systematic audience research and surveys to inform platform formation and campaign plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market analysis and avoid wasted appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: If one section of the community is absolutely sold to the idea of this product, no money is wasted in re-selling it to it. If another section is irrevocably committed to another product, no money is wasted on a lost cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences; focus resources on persuadable groups; use analysis to change or improve the 'product' and decide presentation and media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget campaign expenses and plan fundraising
rubrics_metrics.description: A political campaign should be similarly budgeted. The first question which should be decided is the amount of money that should be raised for the campaign. Then the second question of importance is the manner in which money should be raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful analysis of campaign costs and business precedents to set fundraising targets; conduct money-raising candidly and publicly (modeled on charity drives) to improve prestige and public interest; eliminate opaque 'black bag' elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate spending according to proportional importance
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a clear decision as to how the money is to be spent. This should be done according to the most careful and exact budgeting, wherein every step in the campaign is given its proportionate importance, and the funds allotted accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate advertising, posters, motion picture exploitation, speeches, spectacular events, etc., proportionately with the budget and the overall plan; some expenditures are warranted only if they remain a small part of the budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional appeals must be integrated with overall plan
rubrics_metrics.description: To appeal to the emotions of the public in a political campaign is sound—in fact it is an indispensable part of the campaign. But the emotional content must (a) coincide in every way with the broad basic plans of the campaign and all its minor details; (b) be adapted to the many groups of the public at which it is to be aimed; and (c) conform to the media of the distribution of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unrelated, haphazard emotional events that become maudlin or wasteful; emotional acts must be part of a conscious coherent whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use varied emotional appeals and media, not words alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Big business has realized that it must use as many of the basic emotions as possible. The politician, however, has used the emotions aroused by words almost exclusively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ pictures, motion pictures, lectures, speeches, music, songs, posters, circulars, and other channels to reach different senses and emotional triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic gestures must epitomize a definite plank
rubrics_metrics.description: The candidate who takes babies on his lap, and has his photograph taken, is doing a wise thing emotionally, if this act epitomizes a definite plank in his platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbolic actions (e.g., kissing babies) must represent and be synchronized with real policy positions; otherwise they are mere haphazard staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize program and ability over personality
rubrics_metrics.description: An entire party, a platform, an international policy is sold to the public, or is not sold, on the basis of the intangible element of personality. ... The party and its aims are certainly more important than the personality of the candidate. Not personality, but the ability of the candidate to carry out the party's program adequately, and the program itself should be emphasized in a sound campaign plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personality as a supporting element only when it helps to present the program; develop and communicate the program's substance clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design appeals around social groups and group leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: The public is made up of interlocking groups—economic, social, religious, educational, cultural, racial, collegiate, local, sports, and hundreds of others. ... The political campaign having defined its broad objects and its basic plans, having defined the group appeal which it must use, must carefully allocate to each of the media at hand the work which it can do with maximum efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify groups, map their interests, enlist or contact group leaders, and tailor messages to align with each group's personal interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a wide variety of events and dramatizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Actually there are infinitely more varied events that can be created to dramatize the campaign, and to make people talk of it. Exhibitions, contests, institutes of politics, the cooperation of educational institutions, the dramatic cooperation of groups ... may be made the vehicle for the presentation of ideas to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create spectacles, exhibitions, coordinated events and educational activities to generate spontaneous public interest before direct appeals are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synchronize all media and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: All these [media] must be employed by the political party if it is to succeed. One method of appeal is merely one method of appeal ... one dare not put all one's eggs into one basket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every medium (printed word, pictures, radio, speeches, events) is coordinated so messages are consistent and mutually reinforcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-depend on news reporters; create newsworthy circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper man looks to him for news. ... By his power of giving or withholding information the politician can often effectively censor political news. ... The political leader must be a creator of circumstances, not only a creature of mechanical processes of stereotyping and rubber stamping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage events and create situations that compel coverage rather than waiting passively for reporters to supply publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use propaganda strategy: dramatize, then answer
rubrics_metrics.description: If he were a propagandist ... he would use [the radio] as one instrument of a well-planned strategy. ... He would dramatize the issue ... In whatever ways he dramatized the issue, the attention of the public would be attracted to the question before he addressed them personally. Then, when he spoke ... he would be answering the spontaneous questions and expressing the emotional demands of a public already keyed to a certain pitch of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the public receptive by staging demonstrations/exhibits/agitations so that subsequent direct communications meet an already primed audience, avoiding argumentative assault on inattentive listeners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer leading the public to following trial-and-error feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: A politician often sends up his balloon ... waits for reverberations ... On the basis of these repercussions he then publicly adopts his original tentative policy, or rejects it. It is a method which has little justification. If a politician is a real leader he will be able, by the skillful use of propaganda, to lead the people, instead of following the people by means of the clumsy instrument of trial and error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use planned propaganda to shape opinion rather than relying on preliminary feelers and reactive policy shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set clear objectives and manipulate circumstances with exact knowledge of the public
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole basis of successful propaganda is to have an objective and then to endeavor to arrive at it through an exact knowledge of the public and modifying circumstances to manipulate and sway that public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine defined goals with detailed audience insights to design interventions that produce the desired shifts in opinion or behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure propaganda is true and social to remain effective
rubrics_metrics.description: The only propaganda which will ever tend to weaken itself as the world becomes more sophisticated and intelligent, is propaganda that is untrue or unsocial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dishonest or antisocial messaging; truthful, socially responsible propaganda retains effectiveness as publics grow more sophisticated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a message the public is receptive to (fertile ground required)
rubrics_metrics.description: There has to be fertile ground for the leader and the idea to fall on. But the leader also has to have some vital seed to sow. ... Propaganda is of no use to the politician unless he has something to say which the public, consciously or unconsciously, wants to hear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate that the chosen message resonates with existing public needs or latent desires before investing in large-scale propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train political leaders and staff in propaganda technique
rubrics_metrics.description: I should have taken some of my brightest young men and set them to work for Broadway theatrical productions or apprenticed them as assistants to professional propagandists before recruiting them to the service of the party. ... The political leader of to-day should be a leader as finely versed in the technique of propaganda as in political economy and civics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide hands-on training, apprenticeships with professional propagandists, theatrical/PR experience, and technical education in persuasion for future leaders and campaign staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutionalize public-relations functions in government
rubrics_metrics.description: There should, I believe, be an Assistant Secretary of State who is familiar with the problem of dispensing information to the press ... The United States Government should create a Secretary of Public Relations as member of the President's Cabinet. The function of this official should be correctly to interpret America's aims and ideals throughout the world, and to keep the citizens of this country in touch with governmental activities and the reasons which prompt them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create official offices staffed by trained technicians to analyze public thought, advise senior officials, and ensure transparent dissemination of significant information; interpret government to the people and people to government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use propaganda continually as an administrative tool
rubrics_metrics.description: But campaigning is only an incident in political life. The process of government is continuous. And the expert use of propaganda is more useful and fundamental, although less striking, as an aid to democratic administration, than as an aid to vote getting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply propaganda methods to ongoing governance—to maintain public understanding, focus attention on policy, and regiment complex publics toward intelligent action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize civic groups (e.g., women's organizations) to map programs and use modern techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Women's most obvious influence is exerted when they are organized and armed with the weapon of propaganda. In Washington they are organized as the Legislative Committee of Fourteen Women's Organizations ... These organizations map out a legislative program and then use the modern technique of propaganda to make this legislative program actually pass into the law of the land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form coordinated organizational structures, publish literature, run correspondence courses, conduct demonstration classes and citizenship schools, and use exhibits and direct-action techniques to mobilize support for legislative goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage experienced professional organizers and veterans of prior movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Possibly the effectiveness of women's organizations in American politics to-day is due to two things: first, the training of a professional class of executive secretaries or legislative secretaries during the suffrage campaigns ... secondly, the routing over time activities of the many prominent women who were in the suffrage campaigns and who also devoted themselves to important drives and mass influence movements during the war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop professional staff and leverage experience from earlier large-scale social movements to increase effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use practical, community-focused educational activities to influence public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: A club interested principally in homemaking and the practical arts can sponsor a cooking school for young brides and others. ... A movement for the serving of milk in public schools, or the establishment of a baby health station at the department of health will be an effort close to the heart of a club devoted to the interest of mothers and child welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponsor locally relevant programs (cooking schools, health stations, cooperative radio programming) that both serve the public and build support for broader policy goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exhibits and demonstrations as persuasion tools (example: tariff exhibit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Consumers' Committee of Women ... rented an empty store ... and set up an exhibit of merchandise tagging each item with the current price and the price it would cost if the tariff went through. ... Hundreds of visitors to this shop rallied to the cause of the committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create concrete, visual demonstrations that make abstract policy impacts tangible to the public; such exhibits can recruit supporters and dramatize issues effectively.
